(p-194) The Surah of Muhammad, upon him be the most excellent prayers and peace. It is also called "The Fighting" (al-Qital), and it is also called "Those Who Disbelieve" (al-Ladhina Kafaru).

Its purpose is to direct the believers to guard the enclosure (hazirat) of the religion (al-din) by sustaining jihad against the disbelievers, until they are compelled to submission (al-sagar), or their misguidance is nullified, just as God has nullified their deeds. This applies especially to the people of apostasy (ahl al-riddah, i.e., those who abandon Islam), who have strayed from the encompassing sphere of the religion into the valleys of manifest error. It also applies to upholding this noble disposition until war lays down its burdens, with all the people of the earth becoming Muslim at the descent of Jesus, peace be upon him. This is indicated by its name ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾, because it is known that whoever bars you from His path, you fight him; and if you do not fight him, you become like him. Its name "Muhammad" is also clearly relevant to this, because jihad was the disposition of the Prophet, upon him be the most excellent prayers and peace, until God took him, while he was the Prophet of Mercy in the time of the great battle (al-malhamah). This is because praise (hamd) does not occur where there is some kind of blame, as has already been established in the Surahs of Fatir, Saba', and al-Fatihah. Whenever there is restraint from the enemies of God, there is blame. The clearest of its names for this purpose is al-Qital (The Fighting).

For the people of misguidance, it is known that: "In the name of God" is the Greatest King, who has established His army to repel [threats] from His sacred domain; "the Most Gracious" (al-Rahman), whose mercy is all-encompassing, at times through explanation and at other times through the sword and the lance; "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahim), who has singled out His party for protection on the road to the Gardens.

* *

When God, glorified is He, established the proofs in the Hawamim (the Surahs beginning with ḥā' mīm) until they became like the sun, from which none deviates except one who is destroyed, and concluded by saying that after these proofs the defiantly disobedient people will perish, He opened this Surah by defining them, saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾, that is, they concealed the lights of the proofs, having deviated despite knowledge. ﴿And barred﴾, that is, they refrained themselves and prevented others, due to their deep entrenchment in disbelief, ﴿from the path of God﴾, that is, the spacious, straight road which the Greatest King has legislated. ﴿He nullified﴾, that is, He annulled, with a great annulment [that removes both the substance and the trace], ﴿their deeds﴾, which are their spiritual essences, namely everything by which they intend to benefit themselves, whether by gaining benefit or repelling harm, after He had frustrated their evil deeds and corrupted their affairs. Among their deeds are those by which they plot against you. For when those deeds go astray from what they intended, because He, glorified is He, made them lost and wasted, they perish: on one hand, they go to ruin; on the other, they go in a direction other than that for which they were intended, so their desired benefit is nullified, and they become void. So you, remove their sensory spirits by annulling their forms and bodies, by severing their limbs, (p-195) while you are in the utmost boldness against them. For their Lord, who brought them into existence, has already nullified them and has permitted you to nullify them. He knew that there is no good in them, and that one who is harmful by nature is killed by law. Whoever you are able to kill is judged to be disbelieving, and is destined for failure and ruin.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When the Surah of al-Ahqaf was built upon what was mentioned concerning the end of those who denied, fabricated, disbelieved, and transgressed, and the Surah opened with their turning away, it was concluded with what had been repeated of their rebuke and reproach. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33], that is: if they had taken heed from the beginning, the matter of return would have been easy for them. Then He mentioned their being presented to the Fire, up to His saying: ﴿Will none be destroyed but the defiantly disobedient people?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. When He concluded with the mention of their destruction, He opened the next Surah with the swift consequence that befalls them in this world. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, [strike] at the necks, until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them, then bind firmly the bonds; then either [release them] as a favor or [take] ransom until the war lays down its burdens﴾ [Muhammad: 4], and so on. This follows the opening of the Surah with His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar from the path of God, He nullifies their deeds﴾, thereby alerting that the root of their trial is only (p-197) what God willed for them in His prior knowledge, so that the believers may know that guidance and misguidance are in His hand. He indicated both paths by His saying: ﴿He nullified their deeds﴾, and by His other saying: ﴿He removed from them their misdeeds and set right their condition﴾ [Muhammad: 2]. Then He made clear that had God willed, He would have avenged Himself upon them, but He commanded the believers to fight them as a trial and a test. Then He urged the believers to do what He had commanded them, saying: ﴿If you support God, He will support you﴾ [Muhammad: 7]. Then the verses were joined together. End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 2:

When he mentioned the people of disbelief, referring to them by their lowest rank so as to include those above them, he mentioned their opposites in the same way, so as to encompass whoever among them belonged to all the groups. Thus the Exalted said: ﴿And those who believed﴾, that is, who affirmed faith with the tongue, ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾, that is, complete deeds in prayer, by founding them upon faith, confirming their claim. Since this description does not belong only to the followers of Muhammad ﷺ, He specified them by His saying: ﴿and believed﴾, that is, in addition to that.

Since some of them, such as Huyayy ibn Akhtab and those who followed his path, had criticized the Qur'an for being revealed in installments (munajjaman), although the Torah was not revealed except in that manner, and none of them is able to deny this, He said: ﴿in what has been sent down﴾, that is, by the One who sends down nothing but Him, in installments, separated, so that after believing in it in general, they would renew their faith in each installment of it, ﴿upon Muhammad﴾, the Prophet, the unlettered, the Arab, the Qurashi, the Meccan [then] the Medinan, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel ﷺ. [Since this indicates that no faith is valid unless it is joined with faith in him ﷺ, it is not accounted of value.] He inserted between the subject and its predicate what makes its reason understood, as an exhortation to it and an emphasis upon it, so He said: ﴿And it is the truth﴾, that is, this which was sent down upon him ﷺ is distinguished by being ﴿the truth﴾, that is, perfect in truthfulness, such that it is abrogated and not abrogated, being ﴿from their Lord﴾, the One who benefits them by sending him. As for His benevolence toward His community, it is evident; as for the rest of the nations, it is by his being the one who intercedes for them with the Great Intercession on the Day of Resurrection, and his community is the witness over them.

Since it has thus been established that they are the most deserving of people of the truth, He explained what this produced for them, indicating that no one can measure God with His due measure, so creatures have nothing but pardon; for they, even if they strive in reform, it becomes apparent to them, due to their deficiency, that they have evil deeds or lapses. So the Exalted said: ﴿He will remove﴾, that is, He will cover with a great covering ﴿from them﴾ in both abodes, through their repentance and their faith, for repentance wipes out what came before it, as faith does, ﴿their misdeeds﴾, that is, the evil deeds that befell them before that, through what appears to them of the good and the guidance of their deeds. Since whoever does evil fears its consequence, and so his thought becomes scattered, for there is no life for one who is afraid, the Exalted said: ﴿and sets right their state﴾, that is, the place of their secret and their thought, with security, success, rectitude, soundness of understanding and right guidance, for what He enables them to of good deeds, and by which their name is made good in both abodes. Ibn Burjan said: When that is set right in the servant, what enters into him, what goes out from him, and what remains in him are all set right; and when it is corrupted, it is the opposite of that. For this reason, when the state of mind is preoccupied, one benefits nothing from the qualities of the inner self. It is known that the verse is of the device of ihtibak: He mentioned the misguidance of the disbelievers first, as evidence of the intention of guidance for the believers second, and the setting right of their state second, as evidence of [the omission of] its corruption first.

Since the recompense is of the same kind as the deed, he gave the reason for what preceded concerning the two groups, saying: ﴿That﴾, i.e., the great matter mentioned here of the recompense of the two groups, ﴿is because﴾, i.e., due to the fact that ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, i.e., concealed the mirrors of their minds, ﴿followed﴾, i.e., with the utmost of their effort and their struggle against what their original natural disposition (fitra) led them to, ﴿falsehood﴾: an action that has no reality outside to correspond to it. This is innovation (ibtida') and inclining after desire (hawa), preferring base enjoyments, so they went astray. ﴿And that those who believed﴾, i.e., even if they were in the lowest degrees of faith, ﴿followed﴾ (p-200) i.e., with the utmost of their effort, pursuing what the original natural disposition calls to, opposing the impulses of appetites and the motives of base enjoyments, however numerous and strong they are, ﴿the truth﴾, i.e., that which has a reality corresponding to it. This is wisdom (hikma), which is acting in accordance with knowledge, and knowledge is the recognition of the known as it actually is. ﴿From their Lord﴾, who did good to them by bringing them into existence and by what caused them to hold sound belief, so they were guided.

Since it is known from this that the inner state of those who disbelieved is falsehood, and the inner state of those who believed is truth, and it has preceded in al-Baqara that a parable (mathal) is what is obtained in the inner perception of the realities of perceptible things, and so it is subtler than the perceptible thing, and that this is the aspect of resemblance, it is known that the parable of each of the two groups is what is known of its inner state. So the parable of the first is falsehood, and the parable of the second is truth. Therefore, He, glorified is He, said, as a resumed statement in answer to one who might say, from the bewilderment of the intellect at what it perceived of the elevation of this discourse: "Is a parable like this to be struck?": ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., in the manner of this matter of great significance, ﴿God strikes﴾, [i.e.,] He who has encompassing knowledge of all attributes of perfection, ﴿for the people﴾, i.e., for everyone who possesses the capacity for agitation and motion, ﴿their parables﴾, i.e., the parables of their own selves and the parables of (p-201) the two aforementioned groups, or the parables of all things whose parables they need to have explained, clarifying them with this same clarity, so that each one takes the recompense of his state. From this parable it is known that whoever follows falsehood, God leads his deed astray, multiplies his evil deeds, and corrupts his affairs; and whoever follows truth and acts by it has the opposite of that, whoever he may be. This is the utmost encouragement to seek knowledge in the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ) and to act upon both of them.

When al-Biqa'i had established that the disbelievers are the most deserving of all creation of nonexistence, because falsehood is their likeness and the reality of their state, he made the following statement its consequence: ﴿So when you meet﴾, that is, O believers, ﴿those who disbelieve﴾, even with the least kind of disbelief, in whatever place and at whatever time it occurs. Since the intended meaning is killing in its most evident and certain form, he expressed it by a verbal noun that denotes the act, which is more concise and emphatic, depicting it in its most abhorrent form, along with the severity toward the disbelievers and the contempt for them. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿then striking of the necks﴾. That is, they should follow your encounter with them without delay by striking their necks, striking truly, with what takes away their lives. This is seizing the opportunity and acting with the greatest caution. Likewise, the self, which is the most hostile enemy, when you overcome it, you must not leave any remnant of it. Al-Qushayri said: "When a snake is left with some remnant, and a finger is placed upon it, it spreads its poison into the finger."

Since the implied meaning was: "This shall remain your action," He connected it with His saying ﴿until﴾, and gave good news by using the particle of certainty, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿when you have inflicted heavy losses upon them﴾, that is, you have made the killing severe and abundant among them, to the point that they have no movement left, like one who is heavily wounded, whose wounding has become excessive. So He made this a condition for taking captives, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for a prophet to have captives until he inflicts heavy losses in the land﴾ [al-Anfal: 67]. Then He said, exalted is He, explaining what follows the inflicting of heavy losses: ﴿then bind firmly﴾, that is, because there is now nothing preventing you from taking them captive, ﴿the bonds﴾, that is, the restraint by which they are securely held as captives, by binding their hands together to their necks. This is a metaphor for taking captives to the utmost degree of dominance and subjugation.

Since the Imam (the ruler or head of state) has the choice concerning their captives among four things: killing them, releasing them freely, releasing them for ransom, which is something he takes in exchange for their freedom, and enslaving them, He expressed this in detail by His saying: ﴿then either generosity﴾, that is, that they show them grace in kindness, ﴿afterward﴾, that is, at all times after the capture, by sparing them. Then, after the grace of sparing them, this may be accompanied either by enslavement or by release. Then release is either free, ﴿or ransom﴾, for property, or in exchange for Muslim captives, or the like. The expression "generosity," whose meaning is grace, indicates that sparing is not obligatory in every case. Three forms fall under sparing: enslavement, free release, and release for ransom. He, glorified and exalted, expressly mentioned ransom, whose meaning is taking, in a way that makes it a counterpart to generosity. So it is known that by sparing is meant leaving alive without taking anything. This includes free release, which is clear, and enslavement, because it is a grace compared with killing. The expression "generosity," whose meaning is grace, from al-Mannan (the Bestower of grace), which is one of God's names, and whose meaning is the one who gives without prior obligation, indicates the permissibility of [killing], because grace is optional, not obligatory. For if it were obligatory, it would be a right and not a favor. Thus the four categories are included in the use of these two words. And God is the Guide. All of this is according to what the Imam or his deputy sees as beneficial. Al-Qushayri said: "Likewise is the state of striving against the self: when there is a moment of rest and a day of breaking the fast, it refreshes the self from exertion and gives strength for striving in what is to come, according to what is judged sound by the seeker's shaykh, by the verdict of the tongue of the time, or by the insight of the one who strives." End of quotation.

This context indicates that this ruling is established and not abrogated (naskh, meaning abrogation of a ruling by a later one). The command to killing [alone] in other verses is general and [not] restricted by what the purpose clause indicates, namely that the meaning is: striving in this manner remains valid and continues with every ruler, whether righteous or wicked. A group of the community will always remain standing in it, prevailing upon the truth, not harmed by whoever forsakes them, until God's command comes. This, and God knows best, is what is meant by His saying ﴿until﴾, that is, do what I have commanded you, according to what I have renewed for you, until ﴿war lays down its burdens﴾, and the burdens are its loads, that is, the implements that weigh upon those who bear them, such as provisions, weapons, horses and the like. This does not happen while there is a disbeliever on the earth. That will be in the time of Jesus, peace be upon him, when the earth brings forth its blessings and the religion is one, which is Islam, submission to the Lord of the worlds. Then people will make iron weapons into plowshares, sickles and axes, which they will use in their livelihood. As it occurs in the hadith: "Striving continues [since God sent me] until the last of my community fights the Dajjal." It is narrated by al-Daylami in al-Firdaws from Anas, may God be pleased with him. And: "Striving is obligatory upon you with every righteous and wicked ruler." It is narrated by Abu Dawud from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him.

Since war is hateful to souls and very hard, He emphasized its matter with a statement meaning: this is a matter that has been settled. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That﴾, that is, the great matter, lofty in goodness, beneficial, bringing every good. Since this might give the impression that the emphasis on this matter is because the situation cannot be ordered except by it, He followed it with what removes this impression, saying: ﴿But if﴾. Since if He had expressed it in the past tense it would indicate that it has already happened and ceased, He expressed it in the present tense, which indicates the present state and what follows it, saying: ﴿God willed﴾, that is, the great King, who possesses all attributes of perfection and power over whatever is possible, ﴿He would have taken vengeance upon them﴾, that is, by Himself without anyone else, a great vengeance, by leaving none of them alive. ﴿But﴾ He required this of you ﴿so that He may test﴾.

Since the testing is not specific to one group among them, but general to both groups, because it reveals the people of good qualities and the people of bad qualities from each of them, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿some of you﴾, from the group of believers, by denouncing those from the group of tyrants, so that they may have a white hand in that, ﴿by means of others﴾, that is, He acts in this as one who tests, so that the reward may follow according to what you are accustomed to.

Since this implies that the testing between the two groups is through striving, He said, connecting it to what is implied: "Then those who fought or were killed in the way of Satan, He has caused their deeds to go astray." ﴿And those who were killed﴾. In the reading of the Basrans and Hafs it is "qatalu" (they killed), which is more encouraging, while the first (qutilu) is more hopeful in its effect, ﴿in the way of God﴾, that is, for the sake of facilitating the path of the great King, who is characterized by all attributes of perfection.

Since this is in the context of encouragement, He joined the report with the particle fa' (then), to inform that the cause of their deeds is this, so He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He will not waste﴾, that is, He will not let perish or nullify ﴿their deeds﴾, because they do not follow a proof. Rather, He makes them see the proofs and grants them success in following them. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, as a reason:

(Al-Biqa'i, Nazm al-Durar, on Surah 47, verse 5)

﴿He will guide them﴾ meaning: in both abodes, by a promise that admits no failure, after striving, to everything that benefits them, renewing this continually and steadily. ﴿And will set right their affairs﴾ meaning: the place of their thought; He makes it prepared for every good, far from every evil, safe from fears, and at peace through faith with what it contains of tranquility. So if anyone among them is killed in His cause, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, takes charge of his heirs in a better manner than the way the one killed would have managed them had he been alive.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 6:

When this was a great reward and a bountiful gift, He followed it with a greater reward than it, so the Exalted said: ﴿And He will admit them to Paradise﴾, that is, the abode of settlement, complete in bliss. He answered one who might ask about how they would be admitted to it and what it would be like at that time, with His saying: ﴿He has made it known to them﴾, [that is,] by making known the deeds that lead to it (p-208) and by granting them success in reaching it in this world. Also, by showing them their stations in the Hereafter, so that each one of them becomes more knowledgeable of his station there than of his station in this world, and by the goodness of its fragrance, the elevation of its place, and the height of its walls, for it has lofty chambers and elevated halls. In this verse there is a great good news for one who strives (jihad, struggle in the way of Allah) even for a moment: that Allah will cause him to die upon Islam, which entails that no deed of his will be lost. This is supported by what al-Tabarani narrated in al-Kabir from Fadalah ibn Ubayd al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "For Islam there are three houses: a lower one, an upper one, and an upper chamber. As for the lower one, Islam has entered it, the general body of Muslims, so do not ask any of them without him saying: 'I am a Muslim.' As for the upper one, it is the varying degrees of their deeds; some Muslims are superior to others. As for the upper chamber, jihad in the way of Allah, none attains it except the best of them."

When he mentioned fighting, the listener became eager to know the state of the fighter in terms of victory and defeat, so He answered with what is known as the condition for victory, saying: ﴿O you who have believe﴾, meaning: those who have affirmed this, even if at the lowest of levels, as indicated by the distancing particle (p-209) and the past-tense relative clause. ﴿If you support Allah﴾, meaning: a continuous intention and constant action will renew for you in supporting the religion of the Greatest King, by clarifying its proofs and making them manifest, by exposing the doubts of the people of falsehood and fighting them, and this should be purely for Him and not for any other corrupt intention tainted by seeking worldly gain, or fame for bravery and knowledge, good repute, zeal for one's people, or anything else. ﴿He will support you﴾, for He is the Supporter, not anyone else, whether by number or by equipment, and He will subdue the enemies of the religion by your hands.

Since victory may come along with weakness, laziness, cowardice and failure, He explained that He protects them from these, saying: ﴿And He will make your feet firm﴾, meaning: a great firmness, by filling your hearts with tranquility and assurance, and your bodies with strength and courage at the time of killing, during disputation and argument, and while engaging in all actions, so that you will be dominant [overcoming] in the utmost state of good souls and expanded hearts, with trust in Allah and reliance upon Him, even if all the people of the earth band together against you.

When he mentioned the people of faith, he explained what awaits the people of disbelief. So He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, meaning they concealed what reason indicates and what the original innate dispositions (al-fiṭar al-ūlā) lead to. He also made clear that the evil of their deeds is the cause of their ruin, with the particle fa' (بِالفاءِ). Then He said, emphasizing by making the predicate an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq, the accusative of emphasis and kind) in order to express how unlikely their downfall seems given their strength through the abundance of their numbers (p-٢١٠) and their wealth in numbers: ﴿then ruin (fataʿsan) for them﴾. Meaning, they have stumbled, so they are told what is said to one who stumbles and is not meant to rise: "taʿsan lā qiyāma maʿahu" (ruin, with no rising for him). This is like what is said to one who has stumbled when one wants him to get up: "taʿsan [laka]" (ruin for you). Taʿs means decline, abasement, humiliation, and distress.

Since it was as if someone had asked, "For whom is this?", He said: ﴿for them﴾. So they will hardly stand firm in battle against those whose deeds are righteous.

Since a person may stumble and fall, and be told "ruin," and then get up afterward without his deed being nullified, He made clear that His statement is not like that. Rather, whatever He says comes to pass without any exception at all. So He said, using the past tense to indicate that it is certain, whereas the future may allow that He will forgive some of them, linking it to what is implied: so He, exalted is He, said to them that: ﴿and He will render their deeds void﴾, even though they were apparently sound, because they neglected the foundation, which is faith.

ولَمّا بَيَّنَ ما صَنَعَ بِهِمْ لِيَجْتَرِئَ بِهِ حِزْبُهُ عَلَيْهِمْ، بَيَّنَ سَبَبَهُ لِيُجْتَنَبَ فَقالَ: ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ الأمْرُ البَعِيدُ مِنَ الخَيْرِ ﴿بِأنَّهُمْ﴾ أيْ: بِسَبَبِ أنَّهم ﴿كَرِهُوا﴾ بَغِضُوا وخالَفُوا وأنْكَرُوا ﴿ما أنْـزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾ أيِ: المَلِكُ (p-211) الأعْظَمُ الَّذِي لا نِعْمَةَ إلّا مِنهُ، والَّذِي أنْزَلَهُ مِنَ القُرْآنِ والسُّنَّةِ هو رُوحُ الوُجُودِ الَّذِي لا يُعانِدُونَهُ، فَلَمّا كَرِهُوا الرُّوحَ الأعْظَمَ بَطَلَتْ أرْواحُهم فَتَبِعَتْها أشْباحُهُمْ، وهو مَعْنى قَوْلِهِ مُسَبَّبًا بَيانًا لِمَعْنى إضْلالِ أعْمالِهِمْ: ﴿فَأحْبَطَ﴾ أيْ: أبْطَلَ إبْطالًا لا صَلاحَ مَعَهُ ﴿أعْمالَهُمْ﴾ بِسَبَبِ أنَّهم أفْسَدُوها بِنِيّاتِهِمْ فَصارَتْ وإنْ كانَتْ صُوَرُها صالِحَةً لَيْسَ لَها أرْواحٌ، لِكَوْنِها واقِعَةً عَلى غَيْرِ ما أمَرَ بِهِ اللَّهُ الَّذِي لا أمْرَ إلّا لَهُ يَقْبَلُ مِنَ العَمَلِ إلّا ما حَدَّهُ ورَسَمَهُ، وهَذا وعِيدٌ لِلْأُمَّةِ بِأنَّها إنْ تَخَلَّتْ عَنْ نَصْرِ اللَّهِ والجِهادِ في سَبِيلِهِ والأمْرِ بِالمَعْرُوفِ والنَّهْيِ عَنِ المُنْكَرِ وكَلَها سُبْحانَهُ إلى نَفْسِها وتَخَلّى عَنْ نَصْرِها [وسَلَّطَ عَلَيْها عَدُوَّها]، ولَقَدْ وُجِدَ بَعْضُ ذَلِكَ مِن تَسَلُّطِ الفَسَقَةِ لَمّا وُجِدَ التَّهاوُنُ في بَعْضِ ذَلِكَ والتَّواكُلُ فِيهِ.

(p-212) Since no one treats these matters lightly or dares such calamities except one who feels secure from punishment, and no one feels secure from punishment except one who turns away from God, may He be glorified and exalted, and since His recorded dealings with the earlier nations, for rejecting His messengers, opposing His friends, and transgressing His limits, were sufficient to deter from both, He spoke in disapproval and reproach, having already warned them against His seizing and His might, His severe grip and His punishment. This was tied to their aforementioned aversion and to the hostility toward the people of God that followed from it: ﴿Have they not traveled﴾ [i.e.] because of correcting their deeds and building them on a foundation ﴿in the earth﴾, meaning the land in which are the traces of those events, for that is truly the earth, because of the greater knowledge of God it provides ﴿and observed﴾ as a result of their travel and because of it. Since His dealings were a robe of honor for hearts, given the striking matters in them whose signs speak through the state of things after the warning by speech, He brought this forth in the style of interrogation (istifham), in a manner that draws attention to its greatness, so much so that it empties time for attention to inquiring about it. He said: ﴿how was the end﴾, i.e., the final outcome, ﴿of those﴾ and since they could know that from all the destroyed, He indicated by the insertion of the preposition [that they are some of them, rather some of the deniers of the messengers, and they are those who heard their reports and saw their dwellings] of ʿAd, Thamud, Madyan, Saba, and the people of Lot. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿before them﴾. And since it was as if it were said, "What about them?", He said: ﴿God destroyed﴾, i.e., the Supreme King inflicted a great destruction that came in without permission, striking suddenly ﴿upon them﴾, by what He knew of their people, their conditions, and everyone who approved of their deeds or their words. He turned [from] saying, "and for these," to His saying: ﴿and for the disbelievers﴾, generalizing and attaching the judgment to the attribute, namely deep-rootedness in disbelief. In this there is good news that God, exalted is He, will save some of them from the causes of destruction, because he is not deeply rooted in disbelief, for he has not been sealed upon it. ﴿Their like﴾, i.e., the like of this outcome.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 11:

When he had explained that He would exalt His allies and humble His enemies, he explained the reason for it, saying: ﴿That﴾, i.e., the great matter which He did to the two groups, ﴿is because Allah﴾, i.e., because the Greatest King, encompassing all the attributes of perfection, ﴿is the Protector (mawla) of those who believe﴾, i.e., near to those who affirm Him and are pleased with Him. So He does with them, by His majesty and beauty, what a near one does for his beloved near one. Al-Qushayri said: It may be said that this is the most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah, because He did not say "the ascetics, the worshippers, the people of litanies and striving," but rather mentioned the lowest rank of the people of faith.

﴿And that the disbelievers﴾, i.e., those who are deeply rooted (ʿarīq) in this description, ﴿have no protector (mawla) for them﴾ in this sense, because they are far from Allah, who alone is truly worshipped. Thus the nearness of any near one does not benefit them at all, even though Allah is their Protector in another sense, namely that He is their Lord and Owner. This also contains an allusion that He, glory be to Him and exalted, is the Protector of whoever is not deeply rooted in disbelief, so that He brings him out of the darkness into the light.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 12:

When the listener yearned to learn the full effects of the guardianship (wilayah), he said, healing the perplexity of their question and emphasizing because of the abundance of deniers: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses all perfection, ﴿will admit those who believe﴾, that is, those who established belief (tasdiq), ﴿and do﴾ ﴿righteous deeds﴾, as confirmation of their claim that they had established it. So they enjoy what Allah has provided them of pleasures, not as pleasures in themselves, but as things permitted, and they are a provision (balagh) for the Hereafter. They eat not for indulgence but to strengthen the body for what they were commanded, eating for sustenance and not for enjoyment. ﴿Gardens﴾, that is, great orchards described as ﴿flowing﴾, and he showed the nearness of the water to their surface by his saying: ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾. That is, they are constantly growing, bright, fresh, and fruitful, because the roots of their trees are on elevated ground, such that whenever a patch of it is touched by the slightest stirring, a river flows from it. Their entry has made them forget the bitter sorrows they endured in the world, the hardship of life and the suffering of trials. They add its bliss to the bliss they had in the world of union with Allah, and no turbidity whatsoever reaches them. It is their abode, and they seek no change from it. This is in return for what was withheld from them of [the world] and for the narrowing of their livelihood in it, out of His jealousy for them, until He emptied them for His service and bound them to His presence, out of love for them and to honor their destinies. ﴿And those who disbelieve﴾, that is, they covered over what reason indicates, and so they performed for the sake of their disbelief corrupt deeds that distance them from the presence of Allah. ﴿Enjoy themselves﴾, that is, in the world, with pleasures (p-215) because they are pleasures, as cattle enjoy themselves, heedless of what Allah has commanded, turning away from meeting Him, indeed from death altogether. Rather, the mention of death impels them to plunge into pleasures, racing against it, out of ignorance of Allah. ﴿And eat﴾ continuously, ﴿as cattle eat﴾, eating with relish and exuberance, from whatever place and in whatever manner, eating with seven intestines, that is, in all their bellies, without distinguishing the lawful from the unlawful. This is because Allah the Exalted gave them the world, widened their provision in it, and emptied them for it until it occupied them from Him, in contempt for them and hatred of them, since He knew their condition before He brought them into existence, so He will admit them to a Fire whose fuel is people and stones. ﴿And the Fire﴾, that is, while the state is that it has the greatest heat and the burning beyond all bounds, ﴿is their residence﴾, that is, their dwelling and place of abode, ﴿for them﴾, which will make them forget, at the very first immersion in it, every bliss they had, and then no bliss will ever be theirs at all. Rather, punishment will not leave them for any period of time. The verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which elements omitted from one half are implied by their counterparts in the other half). It mentioned righteous deeds and entry into gardens first, as evidence for the omission of corrupt deeds and entry into the Fire second, and mentioned enjoyment and residence second, as evidence for the omission of the pretext (ta'allul) and the refuge (ma'wa) first. Thus it is ihtibak [within ihtibak] (p-216) and ishtibak (a rhetorical interlacing) accompanying an ishtibak.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 13:

When He, glorified is He, promised that He helps whoever helps Him, because He is his Protector (mawla), and admits him into the abode of His blessing, and forsakes whoever opposes Him, because he has been hostile to Him, until He admits him into the abode of his wretchedness, the implied sense (taqdir) served as proof of this: "How many a people, weaker than those who followed you, We helped against those who denied them, so there is none to help them." Then He joined to it His saying: ﴿And how many﴾. And since the power of Quraysh was in reality in their city, and attributing it to them was more indicative of the solidarity of its people and the intensity of their unity, until they were as if they were one thing, [He] said: ﴿of a town﴾, meaning: one that denied its messenger, ﴿which was mightier in power﴾ and greater in numbers ﴿than your town﴾. And since the revelation of this was after the Hijrah, He specified, saying: ﴿which expelled you﴾, meaning: its people expelled you, agreeing on the causes of expulsion, of various kinds of harm, with one word, until their hearts were as one heart, so it was as if it were the one doing the expelling, and it is Makkah. They denied you and harmed you until We expelled you from among them, so that We might help you against them through those whom We strengthened you with from your town, this one that sheltered you, from the Ansar, a help proceeding in accordance with what you are accustomed to and familiar with. ﴿We destroyed them﴾ with the punishment of annihilation, as Our greatness required, and He related their past condition by His saying: ﴿so there was none to help them﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 14:

When this was an observable proof, after the rational proofs for what the promise was previously mentioned for, he made the denunciation of them its consequence, and said: ﴿Is then one who is upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾, that is, in all his conditions, ﴿upon clear evidence﴾, that is, a state clearly manifest in showing that it is the truth, ﴿from his Lord﴾, the Nurturer, the Manager who looks after him and does good to him by establishing proofs that render all creation unable to produce even one of them. So he perceived the badness of his deed, and it was shown to him as it truly is, so he saw it as evil and avoided it, opposing his desire. Al-Qushayri said: The scholars are in the light of their proof, and the gnostics are in the light of their explanation.

﴿Like one for whom the evil of his deed has been made attractive﴾ by the adornment of Satan, through Our giving him power over him and Our creating the consequences from the easiest matter, ﴿the evil of his deed﴾, of polytheism or of a sin short of it.

Since the implied sense is: "so he saw it as good and did it, persisting in it," and so he was in blindness and error, and since he had made the pronoun singular in accordance with the wording of "one who" (man), he gathered it in response to its meaning, by generalizing the ugliness, both dual and singular, and as an indication that [that] the ugly thing is at first very small, and whenever it is neglected and its root is not cut off, it spreads and proliferates. So he said, conjoining it to what I have estimated: ﴿and they followed their desires﴾. So they have no doubt concerning any of their evil deeds, let alone a proof. The verse is of the type of ihtibak (p-٢١٨): he mentioned the clear evidence first as a proof of its opposite second, and the adornment and the following of desire second as a proof of their opposites first. Its secret is that he mentioned the root that gathers all good, as an encouragement, and the root that gathers all evil, as a warning.

[p-219] When the mention of Paradise and Hell had been repeated throughout this surah, it ended with this verse, which divides people into guided allies and misguided, transgressing enemies. Its context points to the implied sense: "Is one who stands upon a clear proof from his Lord, [whom God] has given a good life in both abodes, like one who follows his desire, whom it has led to ruin in them?" Then it followed this with a description of Paradise, the abode of His allies, to which guidance led them, and of the Fire, the abode of His enemies, to which error drove them, since error necessarily leads to destruction. So He said: ﴿The parable of the Garden﴾, that is, the great gardens whose interior is concealed by the abundance of their trees.

Since God, glory be to Him, repeated His promise to those who believed concerning Paradise, sometimes by the all-comprehensive Greatest Name and sometimes by a pronoun referring to it, the promise of it became in the highest degree certain. So He expressed it here in the past tense in the passive voice, indicating that it is a matter that has already been realized with the greatest ease and completed, such that it is now present, and nothing prevents it except the condition on which the promise is contingent. He described it with attributes that establish with certainty that none is able to bring it about except God. Thus the mere mention of it, and the report of it in the passive form, became more exalted in its matter. So He said: ﴿which the righteous have been promised﴾, that is, those whom their piety carried, after refraining from every act for which no proof had been given, to listen to you and benefit from what you guided them to of the matters of religion. Thus people divided into three categories: one who turns to it wholeheartedly and is a follower; one who turns away from it entirely; and one who listens but does not benefit.

Since the implied meaning is: like a great orchard whose leaves never fall, whose fruit never ceases, and whose bounty cannot be fully perceived, because of the diverse rivers within it, and since what is of this description is, for us, something imagined rather than known, He set aside its detailed description and mentioned what indicates it of the attributes of the promised Paradise, which is known through the promise of the Truthful One, whose truthfulness is established by miracles. So He said, as a resumption (*istinaf*): ﴿in it﴾, that is, in the promised Paradise. Since what they are accustomed to of gardens does not contain more than three rivers, He used the plural form which is employed for abundance when a context indicates it, and here the context is praise and bounty. So He said: ﴿rivers of water﴾. Since the water of this world varies in taste among three kinds—sweet, fresh and salty—while the land is one in its flatness and the close connection of its parts, to indicate that the One who does this is capable and chooses; and since it may become *āsin*, that is, changed from the water that is drunk, with a foul smell, either from its original creation or from an accident that befalls it from its source or its course—He said: ﴿unpolluted﴾, that is, there never comes upon it, at any time, any change in taste, smell or color in any way, however long it remains and however much else is added to it, for it does not accept change in any way.

Since most of their drink after water is milk, He mentioned it next, so He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿and rivers of milk﴾. Since change is not praiseworthy, and they were accustomed in this world to know that milk, of all kinds, is good at the moment it comes from the udder, despite the difference of milk-yielding animals in shape, kind, quantity and temperament, and despite each one being separate from the others, and that it only changes after being milked, He expressed it with a form that negates change in the past, saying: ﴿whose taste does not change﴾, that is, by itself, from its original creation, even if it remains for eternity. This implies that if they wanted to change it for a desire they craved, it would change; and that it, despite its goodness, is of many varieties, as it was varied in this world.

Since most of what follows milk is wine, He said: ﴿and rivers of wine﴾. Since the taste of wine is often strong, and drinkers drink it for its effect, and since whenever its taste changes its name disappears, it is known that everything in the wine of Paradise is of the utmost excellence and is not subject to any flaw of taste. So He said: ﴿delicious﴾, that is, having enduring pleasure for those who drink it, both during drinking and after it, ﴿to the drinkers﴾, in the goodness of its taste and the excellence of its outcome.

[p-221] Since honey is the most precious and the least abundant of these, He placed it last, though it is the most exalted. So He said: ﴿and rivers of honey﴾. Since the honey of this world is found only mixed with wax and other impurities, He said: ﴿purified﴾, that is, it is pure with the purity of whatever effort has been made to purify it of such things. This attribute belongs to it permanently, never separated from it at any time. By this, the utmost desire for Paradise has been achieved through the illustration of what people enjoy of the drinks of this world, since this is the utmost of what we know of that, free of anything that diminishes or disturbs it, together with the description of abundance and continuity.

Al-Baghawi said: Ka'b al-Ahbar said: the Tigris is the river of Paradise's water, the Euphrates is the river of its milk, the Nile of Egypt is the river of its wine, and the Sayhan is the river of its honey. These four rivers flow out of the river al-Kawthar. Ibn Abd al-Hakam said in *Futuh Misr*: Uthman ibn Salih narrated to us, Ibn Lahi'a narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, that Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with both of them, asked Ka'b al-Ahbar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Do you find any report about this Nile in the Book of Allah, the Exalted?" He said: "Yes, by the One who split the sea for Musa, I find it in the Book of Allah that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, reveals to it twice every year. It is revealed to it about its flowing: 'Allah commands you to flow.' So it flows what Allah has decreed for it. Then after that it is revealed to it: 'O Nile, flow abundantly.'" Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us, al-Layth narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Abu al-Khayr, from Ka'b al-Ahbar, that he used to say: "Four rivers from Paradise, which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, placed in this world: the Nile is the river of honey in Paradise; the Euphrates is the river of wine in Paradise; the Sayhan is the river of water in Paradise; and the Jayhan is the river of milk in Paradise." Sa'id ibn Abi Maryam narrated to us, al-Layth ibn Sa'd and Abdullah ibn Lahi'a narrated to us, both saying: Yazid ibn Abi Habib narrated to us, from Abu al-Khayr, from Abu Junada al-Kinani, that he heard Ka'b say: "The Nile in the Hereafter is honey, flowing most abundantly among the rivers that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, named; the Tigris in the Hereafter is milk, flowing most abundantly among the rivers that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, named; [the Euphrates is wine, flowing most abundantly among the rivers that Allah named], and the Jayhan is water, flowing most abundantly among the rivers that Allah named."

The origin of all this is what is in the Sahih in the description of Paradise, from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Sayhan and Jayhan, the Nile and the Euphrates, are among the rivers of Paradise." Abu Hayyan said, regarding the wisdom of their order, other than what has preceded: it began with water, which is indispensable among drinks; then with milk, since it functions like food in much of the sustenance of the Arabs and others; then with wine, because when quenching and food have been attained, the soul yearns for what is enjoyed; then with honey, because in it is healing in this world from what afflicts food and drink. End of quotation. Better than this is that, since the context is one of wonder in the striking of the parable, and since this is a statement never free of strangeness, He began with rivers of water, for its strangeness in their lands and their great need for it. Since its remaining free of change is stranger, He negated it. Since milk is less common, and its flowing as rivers was [stranger], He mentioned it second. Since wine is more precious, He mentioned it third. Since honey is the noblest and least common of them, He concluded with it. And He alerted—together with this reminder of His power, exalted be He—to what He wills, with or without cause. These three drinks, one of which is purely a beverage like wine, one of which is predominantly nourishing like honey, and one of which tends toward both, which is milk, all come from water, with their differences in taste and effect in nourishment, medicine and other things. For water is the root of plants, and from plants come milk, wine and honey, through causes that are not hidden. As for the Hereafter, it is free of causes, because His name, glory be to Him, the Manifest, is evident there; for there is no trial in it. By this, another secret of the order is understood: He, exalted be He, placed water first because it is the root of them, and followed it with what is closest to it in drinkability and nature: milk; [then] with what is closer to milk in that it is a drink only; then with honey, because it is furthest from it.

Since fruits are the most delicious of pleasant things after palatable drink, the Exalted said: ﴿And for them therein﴾. Since its inhabitants differ in ranks, the gardens of most of them do not contain all the fruits of Paradise, He made it partial, saying: ﴿of every kind of fruit﴾, that is, all their varieties, in a manner that leaves no need, neither scarcity nor cessation.

Since life does not become pleasant together with the recognition of what would warrant reproach, and He, to indicate that no one can estimate Allah as He truly deserves, because the ranks are dwarfed before His rank, glory be to Him, said: ﴿and forgiveness from their Lord﴾, that is, the One who does good to them by erasing their past sins, both their essences and their traces, such that they fear no consequence of them, neither punishment nor reproach; and [it implies] their failure to reach what is due to Him of gratitude, glory be to Him.

Since this context indicated that the implied meaning is: "Is one who is in this supreme and enduring bliss [like one in Hell?]," He built upon it His saying: ﴿like one who abides﴾, that is, remains in a dwelling without cessation, and He used the singular because abiding encompasses those in it equally. ﴿in the Fire﴾, that is, the Fire whose blaze is not extinguished, whose captive is not released, and whose stranger is not befriended. Since each of its inhabitants has a drink specific to him according to his deeds, and since your Lord does not wrong anyone, the cause of their harm was the drink in the manner that is mentioned, not its coming from a particular source. He built for the passive the phrase, referring to the plural pronoun, the Exalted's saying: [p-225] ﴿and they are given to drink﴾, that is, in exchange for what was mentioned of the drink of the people of Paradise, ﴿boiling water﴾, that is, of the utmost heat, ﴿which cuts their bowels to pieces﴾.

It is possible that this verse contains *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which one term is omitted from each of two parallel parts, each complementing the other). That is because the Exalted, when He mentioned that the believers are in gardens beneath which rivers flow, and that the disbelievers' abode is the Fire, and the implied meaning was His denunciation of one who does not refrain despite warnings, as an alert that his deed is the deed of one who equates Paradise with the Fire—since the Fire being the recompense of one like him and Paradise the recompense of the believer has become a matter that does not permit denial—the sense is: "Is the likeness of the described Paradise like the likeness of the Fire, and is one who abides in Paradise like one who abides in the Fire?" And Allah is the One who grants success in what is right.

Since the implied sense, after this parable, description and encouragement that dazzle the intellects, is: [Among people is one who] listens to you with utmost love and fairness, so Allah elevates him by understanding what is recited, believing in it, acting upon it and relying on it, and these are the God-fearing (muttaqun) who were promised Paradise, He joined to it His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among them is one who listens﴾, i.e., with utmost effort, perhaps he will find in what is recited a flaw by which to cast doubt upon the weak believers. Exalted is He showed their remoteness by His saying: ﴿to you﴾. Since he made the listener singular, looking at the wording "man" (whoever), indicating the paucity of listeners, he made it plural, looking at its meaning, indicating the multitude of the averse, the obstinate, and the mockers among those who listen to him and those who hear him. So Exalted is He said: ﴿until﴾, i.e., and their striving with themselves through listening continued (p-226) until ﴿when they went out﴾, i.e., the listeners and the hearers all together, ﴿from your presence, they said﴾, i.e., both groups, in blindness, feigned ignorance and mockery. Since merely attaining beneficial knowledge is felicitous, he indicated its magnification by building the verb in the passive form for what has not named its doer, so He said: ﴿to those who were given knowledge﴾, i.e., through Allah's preparing them with what He gave them of clarity of understanding, owing to their freedom from the self and its appetites, and their submission to what the primordial nature (fitrah) calls for: ﴿what did he say﴾, i.e., the Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿just now﴾, i.e., before we parted from him and left him, from an hour, i.e., the first time, that drew near to him, from the beginning (inaf) of the prayer, with vowel-movement (tahrik), which is its onset and first part. Abu Hayyan said: it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥal), i.e., "beginning," meaning: what is the speech he has just begun before we separated from him. He rejected its being an adverb (ẓarf) of time, on the grounds that it is an explanation of meaning, and that no grammarian has counted it among the adverbs. [And] al-Baghawi said: I began the matter (ibtada'tuhu), and the anaf of a thing is its first part. Muqatil said: That was because the Prophet (ﷺ) was delivering a sermon and censuring the hypocrites, and when they left the mosque they asked, mockingly, Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "What did Muhammad (ﷺ) say?" Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I too have been asked, among those who were asked."

Since this indicates, of both the one who listens attentively and the one who turns away, the utmost of stubbornness, which indicates the utmost of wretchedness, it produced His saying: ﴿Those are they﴾, i.e., specifically these remote ones from understanding and from every good, ﴿whom Allah has sealed﴾, i.e., the Supreme King, whose greatness has no limit, Exalted is He, ﴿upon their hearts﴾, i.e., so they did not believe and did not understand with the understanding that benefits. For such stubbornness does not occur except through this. Since the implied sense was: they went astray until they became like cattle, He conjoined to it what is among the actions of cattle, so He said: ﴿and they followed﴾, i.e., with utmost effort, ﴿their desires﴾, i.e., departing from the restraint of reason and the inhibition of manliness. Therefore they are careless toward the greatest speech and are eager to gather the trash of this world. Thus they are the people of the Fire, indicated before the verse "the parable of Paradise" by the statement that their evil deeds were made attractive to them.

When he had mentioned what they were upon and condemned them with the most disgraceful mention, he mentioned those who were given knowledge, and said: ﴿And those who were guided﴾, meaning they strove, by listening to you, to obey the call of the original nature (fitrah) to reach guidance, with sincerity in faith (iman), submission and surrender, through various kinds of striving. ﴿He increased them﴾, meaning God, who sealed the hearts of the ignorant, ﴿in guidance﴾, by expanding their breasts and illuminating them with the lights of direct witnessing, so that they became vessels for wisdom. ("Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord guides them by their faith.") ﴿And gave them their taqwa (God-consciousness)﴾, meaning He made clear to them what deserves to be feared and enabled them to avoid it, opposing their desires (p-228). They are the first category of the verse that prepares the parable: ("Are those who stand upon clear proof from their Lord...") The sense of the idafah (possessive construction, "their taqwa") is that He gave each of them a share of it according to what his condition required. Ibn Burjan said: "Taqwa is the work of iman just as the deeds of the limbs are the work of Islam." End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 18:

Since the most dreaded thing to guard against is the Resurrection, which they deny, he (Allah) connected to their following of their desires His saying, ﴿So are they waiting﴾, that is, expecting, but He used it in an unqualified form to indicate how near it is, ﴿except the Hour﴾. Since it was as if it had been said, "What are they waiting for regarding it?", He substituted for it His saying, ﴿that it come upon them﴾, that is, that it arrive over them, and He expressed it by "coming" to add to the frightening. ﴿Suddenly﴾, that is, unexpectedly, without their being aware of it and without preparation for it.

Since that indicates even greater nearness, and since the arrival of the signs of a thing is a stronger indication of its nearness together with an indication of its greatness, He said, giving the reason for the suddenness: ﴿Indeed, there have come﴾. He indicated strength by making the verb masculine, so He said, ﴿there has come its signs (ashrat)﴾, that is, its signs (ʿalamat) which give warning of it, ﴿from the sending of the Prophet (ﷺ)﴾. [The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two."] ﴿The splitting of the moon﴾, which announces the sign of the sun rising from its west, and other things. The subsequent arrival of a thing's preliminaries is nothing but its presence.

Since the coming of the Hour is among its terrors, it (the Hour) is remembered before it descends, so that one acts in accordance with what remembrance requires. And since, when it comes, it preoccupies one from everything else, He connected to its coming His saying, ﴿Then how⦆ — that is, how and from where — ﴿for them when it comes to them﴾, that is, the Hour and its specific signs, like the sun rising from the west, ﴿will there be remembrance for them?﴾ Because they are in the most absorbing of preoccupations, and if they were free, they would not remember and act, so that it would benefit them. Their time for works and its condition, which is acting upon belief in the unseen, will have passed. Likewise is the Hour of a person that concerns him specifically, which is his death, and its signs that compel remembrance, which are sickness, gray hair and the like. Among its specific signs, with which action no longer benefits, is reaching the point of the death rattle (al-gharghara, the rattling in the throat at the moment of death).

When this was known, that remembrance does not benefit once this world, which was made for action, has come to an end, or once the certain signs that disclose it have arrived, He (Exalted is He) attached to it the command concerning the greatest and most noble of creation, the most elevated and most beautiful of them in creation, (ﷺ), so that it would be an obligation (taklif) for others. Thus He, Exalted, said: ﴿So know that there is no god except Allah﴾. That is, the greatest matter, that ﴿there is no god except Allah﴾, meaning that it is greatly negated that there is any worshipped one in truth other than the Supreme King. For this knowledge is the greatest remembrance that saves from the terrors of the Hour. You are only truly a knower when your knowledge is beneficial, and it is only beneficial when it is accompanied by submission and by acting in accordance with what it requires. Otherwise it is pure ignorance. This knowledge also implies that the Hour must necessarily come, because God has promised it, and He is characterized by perfection, and no partner exists who could prevent Him from fulfilling His promise.

Al-Qushayri said: The servant first knows his Lord through proof and argument. His knowledge of Him is then necessary knowledge, and this is the foundation of foundations, upon which every inferential (istidlali) knowledge is built. Then the strength of his knowledge increases with the increase of clarification and the multiplication of proofs, and his knowledge of himself diminishes through the overwhelming of his remembrance of Allah in his heart. When he reaches the state of witnessing and the authority of reality takes possession of him, his knowledge in that state becomes necessary, and his awareness of himself decreases until his knowledge of himself becomes like inference, as if he were heedless of himself or forgetful of himself. It is said: One who sees the sea is overcome by what occupies him in seeing the sea, so that he forgets himself. When he boards the sea, this state grows stronger. When he drowns in the sea, he has no awareness of anything except that in which he is immersed and annihilated.

This phrase (the declaration of faith) contains secrets that fill the horizons. Its four words are composed of three letters, an allusion to the odd (witr), which is Allah (glorified and exalted is He), and the even (shaf'), which is creation, which He brought into being in pairs. Among its letters is one lingual letter and two guttural letters: the hā' and the alif. However, the alif is expressed by its manifestation, which is the hamza, appearing twice and hidden once in the definite article at the beginning. It is mentioned in its own form four times. Thus that makes seven, which is the most complete number for this, and creation was built upon it: the heavens are seven, and the earths likewise are seven. This is an allusion to the fact that the true God, who is pure unseen, is known only through the revelation of His acts. Thus they (the heavens and earths) are a link to knowing Him, and they are divided into the upper and the lower, just as the alif, which is like the unseen since it cannot be pronounced at the beginning, descended in the form of the hamza that is repeated twice in this word, corresponding to the upper and lower worlds, and between them is what we do not know, from what is hidden from us, just as the hamzat al-wasl is hidden.

By expressing the command with this word as "knowledge," he indicates that the act of the heart with it is the greatest foundation. But since its letters are guttural and lingual, this indicates that in regard to it, nothing suffices except the submission of the inner self and the agreement of the outer, which is the tongue. The tongue is the interpreter of the heart. Whenever the tongue does not agree with the heart, where there is no obstacle, its owner is among the people of the verse of the Saffat (sūrat al-Ṣāffāt). Its spoken letters are fourteen letters, corresponding to the number of the heavens and earths, indicating the most holy Essence, which is pure unseen. Its intended referent is the name of majesty (al-Jalāla), which is the true God, glorified and exalted is He. The word of majesty indicating Him has five letters, corresponding to the number of the five pillars of Islam. Its oddness (witriyya) indicates monotheism. He did not make in it anything lip-formed (shafahī), because of the permanence of its constancy, since it is the greatest means of drawing near to Allah and the closest connection to Him together with sincerity. The one who remembers with it can persist in it, and his companion does not know of it at all, because no one else knows what is behind your two lips except through your informing him.

Just as the statement indicated monotheism explicitly through this word, it indicated the word of messengership, without which monotheism benefits nothing, allusively through the naming of the sūra "Sūrat Muḥammad." Thus it is fighting (qitāl), because he (ﷺ) was commanded to fight the people until they declare what the sūra declares of the word of monotheism, which is the sūrat Muḥammad (ﷺ), because monotheism does not benefit without testimony to messengership. Between the two words there is a great degree of agreement that indicates complete unity and embrace. For the letters of each of them, if we look at them in writing, are twelve letters corresponding to the number of the parts of the year, each letter expiating a month. If we look at them in pronunciation, they are fourteen letters that fill the two horizons with light, greatness, awe, majesty and dignity. If we look at them by both views together, they are fifteen, which no station can stop from the Lord of the Throne, the Creator of the two worlds. This is a wondrous secret indicating the legal ruling that neither of the two can be separated from the other. Whoever does not combine them in his belief, his faith will not be accepted.

This sūra was placed first in this respect because it has precedence, and the other was mentioned in al-Fatḥ (the sūra of Victory) after it. This sūra is named "Fighting" (al-Qitāl), and the sūra of the Muhammadan word is named "Victory" (al-Fatḥ), an allusion to the fact that no one fights for these two with sincerity except that victory is granted to him, and no one can oppose him while opposing him except in hypocrisy, in the manner of humiliation and disturbance.

Since the attainment of monotheism, which is the perfection of the soul, necessitates answered supplication, as in the hadith of Abū Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) in al-Tirmidhī and Abū Ya'lā: "No believer supplicates Allah with a supplication except that it is answered for him, so long as it is not sinful or severing of kinship," and so on. He said, instructing that it is obligatory for a person, after perfecting himself, to strive to perfect others, so that there may be cooperation in what the servants were created for:

﴿And ask forgiveness﴾, that is, seek forgiveness from Allah after knowing that He has no equal, by supplicating for Him, and by striving in righteous deeds ﴿for your sin﴾, which is every station [high] from which you have risen to a higher one. Create it yourself from your own soul, [meaning] the one who wronged you, so that you may increase your followers, for uprightness prepares one for leadership.

Since the perfection of the soul leads to the perfection of others, so that he may have a like reward, He, Exalted, said, clarifying this great blessing and immense favor, repeating the governing preposition and expressing it with faith and the attribute, as a notice that even the highest of the community needs this, because no one can truly measure Allah as He deserves to be measured. This is an honor to this community, in that He commanded the intercessor whose supplication is answered to ask forgiveness for them, through supplication and urging striving in righteous deeds, omitting the annexed noun to indicate the need for forgiveness in every state, because of the human deficiency through error and forgetfulness: ﴿And for the believing men and believing women﴾, that is, those firm in faith, because they are the most deserving of people of that from you, since whatever good they did was for you a like reward, and none of them is free from shortcoming in the divine knowledge and acting in accordance with it, or from a lapse.

Since knowing who sins and who does not sin depends on comprehensive knowledge, He said, connecting it to what is implied: ﴿So Allah knows your movements and your rest﴾, openly and secretly, and He knows that you will certainly do what He has made you prone to, of sin. And He forgives whomever He wills of those who strive for the perfection of their souls and the perfection of others, by washing away sins through returning to obedience to the Knower of the unseen. ﴿And Allah﴾, who encompasses all attributes of perfection, ﴿knows your turning about﴾, that is, your turning, its place and its time, ﴿and your abode﴾, that is, the place of your residence and repose, and everything that occurs in it of dwelling at its time, in this world and the Hereafter, from the moment you were drops of semen until that which has no end.

And when the knowledge of God is most clearly shown to encompass what a person conceals, especially when it contradicts what he displays, He says, as proof of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge through the disclosure of the secrets of the hypocrites, conjoining it to ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [Muhammad: 16], and ﴿those who believe say﴾ in a continuous, recurring manner. That is, they claimed this with their tongues, though among them were both the sincere and the hypocrite, while the sincere ones demonstrated the truth of their faith by urging the pursuit of good through the continual renewal of revelation, which is the true spirit: ﴿Why has a surah not been sent down?﴾ This is by way of gradual revelation. He used the passive form to indicate that, in their sincerity of faith, they had come to believe that revelation comes only from God, so that they had no need to state it explicitly. ﴿A surah﴾, any surah whatsoever, so that we may rejoice in hearing it, worship by reciting it, and act upon what is in it, whatever it may be, and so that revelation continues among us, renewed with the renewal of time, which would be more energizing for us and more effective in stirring our resolve. ﴿But when a surah is sent down﴾, that is, a portion of the Qur'an whose revelation has been completed, whether gradually or all at once, and which goes beyond what they sought by being perceptible in that it is ﴿clear and definitive﴾, that is, (p-237) explained, [not] obscured by any kind of ambiguity, and not abrogated (naskh, the annulment of a previous ruling by a later one), because it combines excellences for [every] time and place. ﴿And fighting is mentioned in it﴾ in whatever manner of mention, and the reality is that it is not mentioned except as a clear statement that [it] only increases in obligation and emphasis until the war lays down its burdens. Al-Baghawi said: Every surah in which jihad is mentioned is muhkamah (clear and definitive), and it is the most severe of the Qur'an upon the hypocrites. This is narrated from Qatadah. ﴿You see﴾, [that is] with the eye and with the heart, ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, that is, weakness in religion or hypocrisy, among those who professed faith, who asked for the revelation of the Qur'an, and who had sworn by God with their most solemn oaths: ''If you should command them, they would surely go forth.'' ﴿They look at you﴾ with aversion to what was revealed to you, after they had urged its request. ﴿With the gaze of one who has fainted﴾. Since fainting has various causes, He clarified that this is its most severe form, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿from death﴾, which is the end of fainting. He does not blink his eye, but stares fixedly without blinking, out of aversion to fighting, from cowardice and weakness.

Since this is a matter that is repugnant to humanity, for it estranges one from religion and manliness, He made the strongest threat its consequence, saying, threatening them in the form of a supplication that what is hateful should befall them: (p-238) ﴿Awlā lahum﴾, that is, the greatest inclination, woe, downfall, and stumbling-place of ruin is theirs. ﴿Lahum﴾ means specifically for them. I interpreted it thus because, as was previously discussed at the end of Surat al-Anfal, the root *w-l-y* revolves around inclination. When it takes the form of the comparative (*afʿal al-tafḍīl*), which is the view of most, it conveys severity. Al-Asma'i said: it is a past-tense verb, meaning that what destroys them has come near them, and God has brought them to destruction. Al-Radi said, in the chapter on the definite and indefinite: it is a proper noun used for threat, and it has the pattern of the verb, which is why it is not declined. It is neither a comparative of superiority (*afʿal al-tafḍīl*), nor a verb in the pattern *afʿal*, nor a verbal noun, because Abu Zayd related that the feminine *tāʾ* is attached to it, so they say: *awlāh al-ān* (like *armalah*), and it derives from *walahа al-sharr*, meaning it was joined to evil by a state of affairs. Its acceptance of the *tāʾ* does not harm its pattern, for that belongs to another discipline.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 21:

When it became known, from what has been mentioned of the causal connection, that this supplication against them was due to their previous bad manners in their speech and the ugliness of what appeared of their deeds, there arose an eagerness for what befits them. So Allah, exalted is He, said, in the manner of a scattered and disordered enumeration: ﴿Obedience﴾, i.e., (p-239) from them, ﴿and a known word﴾, i.e., by submission, acquiescence and good compliance, is better for them than what they displayed of love for obedience and what their state revealed of aversion. He made both nouns indefinite so that they would be suitable for magnification and for what is less than it. Then He made the following statement follow from them, attributing it to the matter, which belongs to its people, as an emphasis for the content of the speech: ﴿Then when the matter is resolved upon﴾, i.e., when the fighting mentioned at the beginning of the surah and other commands are enjoined as a firm, determined command, ﴿then if they had been true to Allah﴾, i.e., to the King, the Greatest, whose power and knowledge encompass all, in their statement which they made when asking for a revelation, ﴿it would have been better for them﴾, i.e., than their pretexts and their slipping away from it, sneaking off, on the assumption of the revelation, granting that there is some kind of good in their recoiling from the command and their holding back from it. It is also permissible that ﴿better﴾ be a noun not used as a comparative, so that it is understood that their lying is evil for them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 22:

Since this was a rebuke to them for their slackness regarding the command of Allah, He consequently (sabbaba ʿan dhalika) explained the great corruption that results from that slackness and the ruin of lands and the scattering of servants that it brings about, in the form of a question, shifting from the address (khitab) after the rebuke and threat to the third-person form (ghayba), as an alert to the extreme and utmost degree of His anger. So the Exalted said: ﴿Then, would you perhaps,﴾ meaning: as a consequence of your hastiness, you ask that the King command you with what pleases Him; then, if He answers you and shows mercy to you with what He knows to be the best of things for you, which is jihad, you dislike it, turn away from it, and sit back from it. It is said to you, because of the signs seen in you that indicate weakness of faith: Is there any possibility with you, and do you expect something of the expectation that your state is worthy and fit for the concealment of the knowledge of consequences from you, so that you fear for yourselves?

Since the context is one of blaming turning away from the command, he separated ʿasā (perhaps) from its predicate (khabar) with a conditional clause in which turning away is expressed with the form tafaʿʿala (tawallaytum), indicating, together with the ultimate blame, that one who turns away from the command of Allah turns away from what the primordial, upright nature (al-fitrah al-ūlā al-qawīmah) and sound intellect call to its goodness; so he turns away from it only through striving against his own self. So the Exalted said: ﴿If you turn away,﴾ meaning: by your own selves, from the jihad which your Lord commanded you, the One who made you aware of its benefits to a degree beyond which there is no increase, such that no rational person would abandon it with it, and its abandonment cannot be imagined except on the assumption of supposition, as indicated by the conditional particle; or your turning away occurs through the occurrence of something that made it necessary for you and adorned it in your eyes until you did it. This second meaning is what is intended by the passive form in the reading of Ruways from Yaʿqub.

﴿That you cause corruption﴾ meaning: that you bring about great corruption that continually renews itself from you ﴿in the land,﴾ by fighting that Allah dislikes, is angered by, and becomes exceedingly wrathful toward its doer, and you would be in the utmost boldness against Him. For He who showed you mercy by sending down what was sent down has ruled that whoever is cowardly regarding what pleases Him, out of desire for the Hereafter, becomes bold against what angers Him, out of love for this world. You were in this state in the Jahiliyyah, in raiding one another and the like. ﴿And sever your ties of kinship﴾ severing them greatly, severely, abundantly, widely, and extensively, ﴿your kin.﴾ Thus you would become, by that, mighty against the believers just as you were humiliated before the disbelievers. And the least of what is in your turning away is your forsaking the believing mujahidin, by which it may become a cause for the disbelievers to prevail over them; so you would thereby have combined severing their kinship with losing what benefits used to reach you from them. If, after them, you refrain from killing them, you would, along with what of their good you lost, be the most cowardly of people and the most content with shame. And if you undertake to avenge them, you would be like one who begins to do what he was commanded after it has passed, and how could he do that? From this it is known that whoever enjoins what is good and strives against the people of evil is safe from corruption in the land and from severing kinship, while whoever abandons it falls into both. It is also possible that "tawallaytum" is from wilayat al-amr (holding authority), so the verse would be pointing to the rule of the wicked and warning thereby to do the enjoining of good; and this has occurred and its consequences of corruption and severance have been witnessed, along with the resolutions of sorrows and the evil of conduct.

Since he had explained to them what would happen to those who grow sluggish in obeying God's command—for a king does not mention a possibility regarding something unless it is certain to occur, in order to distinguish his speech from the speech of others—how much more so with the King of kings, who encompasses everything in power and knowledge—He explained their condition which produced that outcome for them. So He said, turning away from them (multafitan 'anhum) as an announcement of anger (idhanan bil-ghadab), addressing one who is naturally disposed to compassion toward God's creatures and mercy for them, to inform him that these people's wretchedness has been decreed, so they are not deserving of intercession on their behalf nor of grief over them: ﴿Those are the ones﴾, that is, the distant and the hateful, ﴿whom God has cursed﴾, that is, the Supreme King has banished them with the utmost banishment, because of their corruption and severing of ties that has been mentioned. Then He attributed to their cursing the statement of the Exalted: ﴿so He has made them deaf﴾ to benefiting from what they hear, ﴿and blinded their eyes﴾ to deriving benefit from what they see. (p-243) Their hearing is not the hearing of reflection, nor their sight the sight of contemplation; so for them there is neither hearing nor sight.

When he informed them of that, and some who did not fully grasp his words might ask about the cause that brings the curse, which produces deafness and blindness, he answered them with His words, rebuking and admonishing them and making the taa' of the tafa'ul form (tā' al-tafa'ul, the reflexive infix) visible, to indicate that what is commanded is directing all determination toward reflection: ﴿Do they not then reflect (yatadabbarūn) upon the Qur'an?﴾ That is: everyone who is capable of reflection should do so with hearts open and expanded, so that they may be guided to [every] good.
