[They should strive] upon the Qur'an, by exerting themselves to think about the Book that gathers every good and distinguishes between every deceptive matter, with the thinking of one who looks at the outcomes of affairs and what necessarily follows from their consequences. Thus they would know that there is no help toward reform on earth, toward maintaining the ties of kinship, toward sincerity to God in adhering to every act of obedience, and toward disavowing every act of disobedience, such as enjoining what is right, including jihad with the sword and what falls short of it. Perhaps the appearance of the taa' indicates that this is among the most evident of the meanings in the Qur'an, so that finding it does not require profound reflection. And God knows best.

Since the interrogative is one of denunciation, its meaning is negation. Being introduced upon a negation, it negates the negation, so it becomes affirmation. It is as if it were said: "Do they renew their reflection in a continuous renewal, so that their hearts may be softened by it and their insight illuminated, and so they refrain from corruption and severing ties?" He balanced this with His words, comparing hearts to chests and indicating that comparison by mentioning what is specific to chests, namely locks: ﴿Or are there locks upon hearts?﴾ Of the hearts of the heedless, for this purpose. He made "hearts" indefinite to signify partiality and belittlement, by magnifying their hardness. ﴿Their locks﴾ That is, the locks that are truly theirs and fit to be attributed to them. Therefore they comprehend nothing, understand nothing, and increase only in dullness and obstinacy, because they are unable to reflect. Al-Qushayri said: "Thus the admonitions of warning do not enter them, and the light of knowledge does not spread over them, so the understanding of the address does not arise for them. When a door is locked, just as nothing enters it, nothing comes out of it; so neither their disbelief comes out nor the faith to which they are called enters." End of quotation.

The idafah (attributive construction) "their locks" indicates that [some] of those who turn away have locks upon their hearts, but these locks are not firmly fixed in them. He, glorified is He, opens them by repentance for them when He wills. As for the first group, there is no readiness in them. In this verse is the greatest incitement to accepting God's commands, especially jihad in His way, and the strongest deterrent against turning away from it. For its essence is that He cursed those who turn away from it, because they do not reflect upon the Qur'an despite its clarity and ease, so that they might know the benefits of jihad that call to it and make it beloved. Thus [as if] their heart were locked. The verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device of mutual omission): (p-245) He mentioned reflection first as an indication of its opposite second, and locks second as an indication of their opposite first. Its secret is that He mentioned first the outcome of good, which guarantees happiness, and second the cause of evil, which gathers wretchedness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 25:

When He, glory be to Him and exalted, had informed about the locks upon their hearts, He clarified the source of that, and so He said, emphasizing it as an alert [for one who does not give it attention] that it is among the things one should be concerned to consider, so that a person may deliver his soul from it, and as a refutation of those who say that this is good: ﴿Indeed, those who turned back﴾, meaning they struggled with their souls against the primordial nature (fitrah) in turning back from Islam. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿on their heels﴾, meaning from among the People of the Book and others. Thus they turned the faces of matters over to their backs, fell into misguidance, and disbelieved.

Since what they are blamed for is abandoning what the Prophet ﷺ brought to them of the Law which Allah, glory be to Him, revealed to him, and not what is in their natural dispositions of religion, for guidance to which the light of reason suffices, and since the blame attaches to them even if their apostasy occurred at the least moment, He established the preposition, saying: ﴿after the guidance had become clear to them﴾, the utmost clarity by which there is no concealment in any respect, and it became manifest to the utmost degree ﴿to them﴾, through the proofs which, because of their extreme manifestness, are free of any need for explicit explanation, ﴿the guidance﴾, meaning that which our Messenger ﷺ brought to them.

Since they had by this burned their own souls and banished them to the utmost distance from every good, He expressed the misleader by what indicates that, and so He, exalted be He, said: ﴿Satan﴾, meaning the one burned by the curse, far from mercy. ﴿Enticed﴾ them, meaning he beautified for them, by his adornment and seduction, which produced in them a slackening in their resolve and a languor in their aspirations, so they went along with him in his purpose in lengthening hope, multiplying the committing of slips, and wishes from all desires and pretexts, after he had made the evil of their deeds appear fair to them, through Allah's empowering him over them. This was because He, glory be to Him, knew of them the state of their primordial nature. ﴿And He gave them respite﴾, meaning He prolonged that and extended it by repeating it upon them over the succession of the two alternations and the passing of the two renewals, until they forgot the admonitions and turned away from the remembrance. This is according to the reading of the majority with a fatha on the hamza and the lam. As for the reading of the Basrans with a damma on the hamza and a kasra on the lam, the meaning is that Allah, exalted be He, is the one who gives respite (al-mumli), that is, who postpones for them by lengthening their lives, pouring out blessings, facilitating wishes, and forbearing from hastening them with punishments, until they became deceived. This also agrees with His saying, exalted be He: ﴿We will lead them step by step from where they do not know﴾ [al-Qalam: 44] ﴿And I give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm﴾ [al-Qalam: 45]. As for the reading of Abu 'Amr with a fatha on the ya', it is a past verb in the passive voice, and the reading of Ya'qub with a sukun on the ya', as a present verb whose hamza is for the first person singular, indicates that the one who gives respite is Allah, glory be to Him and exalted.

When he had explained His empowering Satan over them, he explained the cause, saying: ﴿That﴾, that is, the matter far removed from good and from what clear reason indicates, ﴿is because they﴾, that is, because these who turned away ﴿said to those who hated what﴾, that is, all of what ﴿God has sent down﴾, that is, the Supreme King, sent down gradually according to events, a revelation in which there is an inimitability (i'jaz) of creation in the eloquence of its composition together with the excellence of its vocabulary and its solidity, along with ease of pronunciation, sweetness to the hearing, and harmony with human nature, as every taste bears witness, whether of the dull or of the intelligent, despite their differing degrees of dullness and intelligence. There is also another inimitability for them in the soundness and wisdom of its meaning, a third in its correspondence to the circumstance that required its descent, a correspondence that creatures cannot match, and a fourth in its arrangement together with what was sent down before it of verses, not according to the order of revelation but according to what wisdom required, wisdom before which thoughts shrink and which, out of its majesty, turns the eyes of the sound-sighted away in defeat, insights of those endowed with vision. Those to whom this speech is addressed are, God knows best, those who openly profess disbelief. They said to them, after these proofs of inimitability and the clear, manifest signs that preceded them: ﴿We will obey you﴾ with a true promise that admits no breach ﴿in part of the matter﴾, and that is fighting in the way of God, which was previously mentioned: that when a surah is revealed mentioning it, they become like one who swoons from death. [So you are in safety] from our fighting you ever; for we only submitted for safety for our blood and our wealth. What we love of what is sent down is the granting of security to whoever confesses the word of Islam, and contentment with that outwardly, and the general promise of ease in the lands and expansion in provision, and the like. Thus by this they became disbelievers, for religion is not divisible: whoever neglects one of its fundamentals has neglected it entirely. Restricting it to "part" implies that they would not obey them in the other part, which is the showing of Islam and presenting oneself in the form of peacefulness. All of this is because God Most High created them with a natural disposition (jibilla) in which He prepared them for such things. When they said this, neglecting what He had bestowed upon them of the instinct of reason, they deserved, according to the course of our custom, for their choice of obeying the enemy, while the knowledge of consequences was hidden from them, to be forsaken and to have the enemy empowered over them, so that their outward seizure would be by those whom they obeyed inwardly. Had they held fast to their religion and been with its people as one hand against all others, no enemy would have prevailed over them, nor would any calamity they dislike have struck them with harm.

[p. 249] Since whoever has even the least intellect does not betray unless he thinks his betrayal will remain hidden, so that he may be safe from its consequence, He described the ugliness of what they committed, saying: ﴿And God﴾, that is, they said that while the Supreme King, who encompasses everything in knowledge and power, ﴿knows﴾ across all times ﴿their secret﴾, that is, all of it: this which he revealed about them and other things in their hearts that did not come out on their tongues. Perhaps they themselves did not know it, let alone their statements which their tongues uttered. Thereby it became clear that they have no religion, no intellect, and no manliness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 27:

When Exalted is He had made clear the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of them, He followed it with the comprehensiveness of His power. Exalted is He said, as a consequence of their treachery while they were in His grip, with what is not hidden of what they intend by it, namely the preservation of their own selves from being killed, expressing it by way of interrogation (istifham) to alert that their condition, for which they will be recompensed on account of this deserving, is of such foulness, ugliness and monstrousness that the question about it is warranted on its account: [so He said]: ﴿How then﴾, that is, what will be their state ﴿when the angels take them in death﴾, that is, when Our messengers, namely the Angel of Death and his helpers, seize their souls in their entirety, and convey them to the abode of recompense cut off from all their causes [and their lineages], so that their holding back from jihad in postponing their terms did not benefit them. And He depicted their state at the time of their death (p-250), so He said: ﴿they strike their faces﴾, that is, they continue, in the state of the taking, to strike their ﴿faces﴾, which are the noblest of their limbs, which they withheld from the battle to preserve them [from striking the unbelievers]. And since their state in their cowardice required the striking of the necks, He depicted it in its most hideous form, so He said: ﴿and their backs﴾, whose being struck is the clearest indication of the humiliation and baseness of the one struck. Then, after that, their pains, their punishment and their humiliation continue without end.

Since the ingratitude for blessings necessitates, along with the loss of the blessings, the nullification of the services that preceded, He said: ﴿That﴾, i.e., the matter of great humiliation, is from [the act of] Our messengers [toward them], ﴿because they followed﴾, i.e., they dealt with their original natural dispositions by following, out of obstinacy on their part, ﴿what angered God﴾, i.e., the Most Great King, which is acting upon His acts of disobedience, such as allying with His enemies, opposing His allies, and other things.

Since the performance of what angers [God] may occur while being heedless that it angers Him, He made clear that they were not like that, and the Exalted said: ﴿And they disliked﴾, i.e., by associating others with Him, ﴿His good pleasure﴾, by their disliking [the greatest] causes of His pleasure, which is faith. So they disliked what is below it, namely abstaining from the rest of the acts of obedience, even more, because that is evident to the utmost degree (p-251) of evidence that it angers Him, so its doer, despite that, is not excused for neglecting to reflect upon it. ﴿So He nullified﴾, i.e., because of that, it resulted from it that He corrupted ﴿their deeds﴾, the righteous ones, so He caused them to fall away, such that they retained no weight whatsoever, due to their neglect of the foundation of noble character, such as hospitality to guests, lifting up the weak, almsgiving, manumission of slaves, and other forms of kindness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 29:

When He, glorified is He, had depicted what their betrayal produced in its most repugnant form, it became clear [through it] that what moved them to what they did was nothing but their ignorance and foolishness. This yielded their humiliation through rebuke, so He said, linking it to what is implied by the context: "Know that when they said what angers us, that We know their secret and their private counsel, and that Our power encompasses them, so that they would have prepared themselves for the idea that We would expose to the people what they conceal and seize them with a fierce seizing, and they would thus be the most ignorant of the ignorant." ﴿Am﴾ ("or," introducing a rhetorical question) [they] supposed, through the weakness of their minds, as what the expression of supposing ("ḥusbān") conveys. This was the original form, but He expressed it by what indicates the malady that led them to that, so He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, which, when corrupted, corrupts the whole body, ﴿a disease﴾, that is, a affliction for which there is no cure, a supposition that is in the utmost firmness, as indicated by the emphasis in His, glorified and exalted is He, saying: ﴿that Allah will never bring forth﴾, that is, bring out into the open, He who encompasses the attributes of perfection, for the Messenger ﷺ and the believers, may Allah's good pleasure be upon them (p-252), in the manner of renewal and continuity, ﴿their rancors﴾, that is, their inclination and what they hide within the innermost recesses of their hearts of crookedness, which indicates their grudges, namely that they harbor enmity in their hearts, persisting in it, awaiting misfortunes to seize their opportunity. The matter is not as they imagined; rather, Allah exposes them and unveils their deception.

[p. 253] When it became known from this that His knowledge, glory be to Him and exalted, encompasses all things, and that His power is all-inclusive, the author knew that His majesty, glory be to Him, is dazzling and His might overpowering. So he shifted the speech into this style as an alert to that, joining it to what is implied in the phrase: "Their assumptions have failed and their opinions have gone astray. So We will surely bring out what they strive so hard to conceal, until We leave nothing of it that they wish to hide without uncovering it, making it manifest to the people and clarifying it. For We know them, and We know that about them before We created them. Had We willed, We would have exposed them so that all people would recognize them, and none of them would be hidden from anyone else." Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And if﴾. Its waw may be a waw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl), meaning: "Do they think that, while the situation is that if We willed ..." ﴿We willed﴾, that is, a will came into being from Us now, or before it, or after it.

Since, because of the intensity of their ignorance, they cannot conceive that all their inner secrets are known, and that a human like them could be capable of knowing them, He emphasized His statement: ﴿We would have shown them to you﴾, that is, with a complete sight that removes the veil from you concerning them. ﴿And you would surely have recognized them﴾, that is, your sight of them would be followed by your recognition of them, you yourself specifically, ﴿by their marks﴾, that is, by means of their signs, which We make prominent upon them, overpowering them, in revealing what is in their hearts, against which they cannot defend themselves in any way. He, glory be to Him, did not name them by their names, out of consideration for their relatives who were sincere and safe from trials.

When what was linked to the will, of what was possible for Him in the past and otherwise, was completed, He joined to it what He would reveal of their affairs in the future. So He said, emphasizing it to deny the improbability for those among them who find this improbable, or for those among others who share their sickness of heart, in answer to an implied oath indicated by the lam: ﴿And you will surely recognize them﴾, that is, after this time, a recognition that renews itself according to the renewal of their words, continuing with the continuance of their wicked hearts and their secret dealings, ﴿by the tone of their speech﴾ (laḥn al-qawl), that is, what proceeds from them. Its laḥn is its import, meaning its sense. Its direction (madhhab) and what it indicates and hints at of the like, from its realities to its consequences, and what its matter "will come to" that is hidden from others, [p. 254] and Ibn Burjān said: it is what you incline toward with your tongue, that is, you lean toward it so that your companion may understand you, and you conceal it from those who have no prior knowledge of your intention. According to the precise view, laḥn al-qawl is what appears from the purpose of the speech, the hidden implications of the address, the context of the wording, and the look of the face at the time of speaking, even if the speaker does not intend to show it. But it mostly prevails over him in his state, so he cannot entirely conceal it, even if he relies on it in his speaking. Its reality is a state that reveals the secret, and the display of the inner speech almost contradicts the outward speech, through a hidden condition and meanings that the inner dialogue grasps. He said:

"I have indeed allusively spoken to you, so that you might understand, and the allusion is known to those of sound intellect."

And another said:

"Your two eyes have indicated, from you, to my two eyes, things which, were it not for them, I would not have known."

Abu Ḥayyān said: They had agreed on expressions by which they addressed the Messenger ﷺ, whose outward meaning was good, while they intended by them something ugly. Al-Iṣfahānī said: The one who errs is called laḥin, because he turns speech away from correctness. Al-Baghawī said: Laḥn has two senses: correct and erroneous. The verb from the correct sense is laḥana yalḥanu laḥnan, so one is laḥin, when he perceives something. The verb from the erroneous sense is laḥana yalḥanu laḥnan, so one is lāḥin. Its origin is diverting speech from its proper course. [He said]: After this, no hypocrite spoke in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ without his recognizing him. Al-Tha'labī said: "From Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: After the revelation of this verse, nothing of the hypocrites remained hidden from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He recognized them by their marks. We were once on a military campaign, and among us were seven hypocrites whom people praised. They slept one night, and in the morning there was written on the forehead of each of them, 'This is a hypocrite.'" Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them, gave an example of their speech: "What do we get if we obey?" of the reward. He said: They do not say: "What do we get if we disobey?" of the punishment.

When He, glory be to Him, informed that He knows their outward and inward states, and that He makes them clear to His Prophet ﷺ in the forms of what they conceal of their words, and emphasized this because He knew they doubted it, He confronted them with rebuke, adding to their humiliation, and addressing others generally, to inform that He encompasses all. So He said, joining it to what is implied: "So Allah knows your words." ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, by virtue of what He has of the attributes of perfection, ﴿knows your deeds﴾, all of them, the acts and the sayings, the manifest and the hidden, with a fixed unseen knowledge and a firm witnessing knowledge that renews itself according to their renewal, [p. 256] continuing with that continuance.

And We will surely test you, that We may know those among you who strive (in jihad) and the steadfast, and We will test your reports. [Note: rendering below]

Let me correct that and give the full translation as required.

And when Allah, glorified is He, informed that He makes them known to His Prophet ﷺ, He followed it with the report that He also makes them known to all the believers, saying, emphasizing it because they think they possess a strong disposition and sound intellect by which they can conceal their affairs: ﴿And We will surely test you﴾, that is: We will deal with you as one who tests, by mixing with you through what We possess of attributes of majesty, through severe commands upon the souls, hateful prohibitions to them, and calamities, a mixing that inclines and transforms. Likewise the estimation applies to the two verbs that follow, in the reading of the majority with the nūn, following the first style; and in the reading of Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim with the yāʾ, the pronoun refers to Allah, the Exalted, who encompasses the attributes of majesty that return to subjugation and others, and the attributes of honor that lead to bestowal, so it is in complete agreement with the reading of the nūn. ﴿Until We know﴾ through the testing, a witnessed knowledge which others witness, corresponding to what We knew with unseen knowledge, so that We extract from your inner selves what We have brought into being in you [and fashioned you upon, of which none of you knows] — indeed, you yourselves do not know it with its true knowledge — ﴿those of you who strive﴾ in fighting and in all other deeds, hardships and terrors, in compliance with the command to that effect.

And since the pillar of jihad is patience under what is disliked, He said, emphasizing His command: (p-257) ﴿and the steadfast﴾, that is: in the face of the hardships of jihad and other distresses. Al-Qushayrī said: By testing and trial the substance of men is made manifest; the sincere appears, the hypocrite is exposed, and the deceiver is uncovered. And when He set a measure for knowledge of the essences, He followed it with a probe for the knowledge of the righteous, saying, conjoining with "we will know" in the reading of the majority and with "We will test" in the narration from Yaʿqūb with the waw sukūn: ﴿and We will test your reports﴾, that is: We will mix them, by setting over them one who distorts them, making their goodness ugly and their ugliness pleasing, so that the one who acts for Allah becomes manifest to people, and the one who acts for Satan. For the one who acts for Allah, if he names his ugly deed by the name of good, he knows that this is a kindness from Allah to him, so he is ashamed before Him and returns to Him; and if his good deed is named by the name of ugly and he becomes known for it, he knows that this is gentleness from Allah toward him, lest vanity overtake him or ostentation attack him, so he increases in his goodness. The one who acts for Satan increases in ugly deeds, because his reputation among people is the target of his gaze, and he turns back from good, since it did not bring him to what he intended by it, namely the praise of people for him through the report, and he did not affirm it by Us. In Yaʿqūb's reading there is an indication that the transformation of the state of the one reported after his report becomes known is easier than his transformation before it becomes known. It is related from al-Fuḍayl that when he recited this verse he wept and said: O Allah, do not test us; for if You test us, You will expose our veils and disgrace us.

(p-٢٥٨) Since it is the custom that a person neither punishes nor threatens someone unless that person has harmed him, as has preceded in the report of their punishment and the ugliness of their deeds, preparing the listener for the question about that, He began a new statement, emphasizing it to confirm their assumption that they are the victors over the party of God: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾, meaning: they covered up what their minds indicated from the apparent signs of God, especially after the sending of the Messenger, supported by clear miracles (ﷺ). ﴿And barred﴾, meaning: they refrained themselves and prevented others, adding to their disbelief, ﴿from the way of God﴾, meaning: the clear path which the Greatest King laid down. Since most of the context concerns those who conceal their disbelief, He merged into His statement ﴿and opposed the Messenger﴾, meaning: the one perfect in messengerhood, well known in the utmost degree of knowledge.

Since He, glorified is He, had overlooked the neglect of the rational proof (al-dalil al-'aqli) for divine oneness (tawhid) before the sending, He said, affirming the preposition, to inform that He does not forgive one who wastes it after the sending, even for the briefest time: ﴿after the guidance had become clear to them﴾, meaning: to the utmost clarity through the miracle, such that it became evident in itself, not needing a clarifier from what the Messenger showed of extraordinary signs. Among this is what the earlier divine Scriptures reported.

Since the one who opposes the Messenger is actually opposing the One who sent him, He indicated this by His saying, stripping the Messenger of the particle "fa" (so) to show that the non-existence of this harm (p-٢٥٩) is not a consequence, in the sense that this harm exists whether they acted or did not act, whether they found it or did not: ﴿they will not harm God﴾, meaning: the King of kings, and He did not say "the Messenger," ﴿in anything﴾, meaning: neither much nor little of harm, by what they gathered together of disbelief and obstruction.

Since the implied meaning is: they have only harmed themselves immediately, in that they have tired themselves with what did not avail them anything, He followed it with: ﴿And He will nullify﴾, meaning: He will spoil and render void, by a promise that admits no breach, ﴿their deeds﴾, of the good deeds, because they were built on a foundation that is not firm for the hypocrite, so he only does them for show, and for the open disbeliever on no foundation at all, so none of them benefits them. And among the schemes by which they intend to weaken Islam, We will make their destruction lie in their own plotting, even if they go to great lengths to perfect them. They will produce for them nothing but the opposite of what they intended, equally.

When he had concluded all that preceded, namely the encouragement of the sincere and the warning to the wavering and the false, toward sincerity, and had called to this while making clear that there is no purpose at all in it, but that it is mercy, gentleness, and beneficence [and] from Him, he produced his saying, addressing with a call those who needed to be called by way of a kind of distance, because of their need for that and their failure to hasten to it before: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, that is, who have affirmed with their tongues, ﴿obey Allah﴾, that is, the Greatest King (p. 260), confirming your claim of obeying Him by striving intensely in it, that it is pure. He magnified the Messenger ﷺ by making him singular, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿and obey the Messenger﴾, because his obedience is part of the obedience to the One who sent him. When you do that, you have realized your selves and your deeds, as has passed at the beginning of the surah, so they will be sound, being built upon obedience, through the correction of intentions and the purifying of them, together with excellence toward the outward form, so that the deed may be complete in form and in spirit.

Since obedience may be understood as only the establishment of the outward form, He said, alerting to sincerity so that it may be complete in the perceptible and in meaning: ﴿and do not nullify your deeds﴾, that is, by disobeying the two of them. For good deeds, if one intends by them what does not please the two of them, seeking by them [worldly ends], even though they are at the peak of beauty of form, become a form without meaning. They are then among what becomes ﴿scattered dust﴾, like the conduct of those who displayed faith while concealing opposition by hypocrisy, showing-off, self-admiration, a desire for praise, harm, and the like of the disobediences. However, the context, by its preceding and following text, indicates that disbelief is the greatest thing intended by this. The verse contains *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device of mutual omission, in which each of two contrasting terms is left implicit and indicated by the other): He mentioned obedience first as an indication of disobedience second, and nullification second as an indication of soundness first. Its secret is that He commanded the starting point of happiness and forbade the endpoint of corruption second, because it is greater in forbidding corruption, given what it contains of disfiguring its form and exposing its inner reality.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 34:

When what He had first told about the opponents (al-mushaqqin) showed that they are defeated in this world and losers in the Hereafter, and since the loss in the Hereafter was conditional on a condition, He gave the reason (ta'lil) for what the believers were commanded here regarding obedience, and forbidden regarding the nullifying of their deeds through disobedience, [as an addition] in urging them to what He commanded, with two reasons, each of which is independently sufficient to comply with His command and avoid His prohibition: the first is non-forgiveness, and the second is the nullifying of deeds and wealth by the fact that the world has no reality. He placed the first before the second because the second, namely that the world is play (la'ib), is like a reason that is inherent in what necessitated it. Part of the excellence of teaching is stating the ruling and then explaining its cause with the nearest thing that leads to it or turns away from it. So it is as if it were said: Do not nullify them by barring from the path of God, which is driven by turning toward the world, which is the very essence of falsehood (batil). For if you do that, forgiveness will escape you. This is part of the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, emphasizing its content against their denial: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾, meaning: they committed disbelief by their action, acting as one who conceals what his intellect pointed to of the signs of God, the visible and then the audible, ﴿and bar from the path of God﴾, meaning: the road of the Supreme King, the clear, straight path that leads to everything one who seeks it should aim for, by their persistence in their falsehood and their harm to those who opposed them.

Since this is an ugly matter from many aspects, because of what it contains of opposing the Greatest King, whose might is feared and whose wrath is to be dreaded, and because of abandoning the wide for the narrow, the straight for the crooked, and that which leads to success for that which leads to failure, persisting in it is in the utmost remoteness. He drew attention to this with the particle of delay (ta'arrukhi), saying: ﴿Then they died﴾, meaning: after being given respite in their field by the lengthening of their lives, ﴿while they﴾, meaning: while the state was that they were ﴿disbelievers﴾. Since the greatest cause of nullification is dying upon disbelief, He drew attention to it with the fa' that indicates linking the consequent to the condition and its being caused by it, saying, emphasizing it against their denial of it: ﴿then God will never forgive﴾, meaning: the One encompassing all attributes of perfection that prevent equating the evildoer with the doer of good, ﴿them﴾. So He will not erase their sins nor cover their faults, but will expose their inner secrets, weaken their plotting, and turn them back on their heels in everything they turn over in. This is because they have nullified their deeds by leaving the circle of obedience, so nothing remains for which they could be forgiven. This verse has shown what the verse of al-Baqarah showed, that the nullifying of the deed in the apostate is conditional upon dying in disbelief.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 35:

When He, glorified is He, had mentioned the blame of the disbelievers, that He is against them, and that He nullifies their deeds in this world, in war and otherwise, and concluded that His enmity toward them is decreed and cannot be dissolved (p-263), and that this necessitated boldness against them, He followed it with His saying, encouraging them to hold fast to jihad (struggle in the way of God, here including armed fighting) and warning them against abandoning it: ﴿So do not weaken﴾, meaning, do not become so feeble that it leads you to humiliation and abasement, ﴿and call﴾, meaning your enemies, ﴿to peace﴾, meaning reconciliation, which is settlement, ﴿while you are﴾, meaning while the state is that you are ﴿the superior ones﴾ over everyone who opposes you, because God is with you. Then He conjoined to this state His saying: ﴿And Allah﴾, meaning the Supreme King who cannot be overcome by anything and has no equal, ﴿is with you﴾, meaning by His help, His aid, and all that the generous one does when he is with another. Whoever knows that his master is with him, and knows that He is capable of what He wills, will not be concerned about anything at all. ﴿And He will not deprive you of your deeds﴾, [meaning] so that He would strip them from you and leave you as those deprived of them, in the sense that He would nullify them, as He does with your enemies in nullifying their deeds, so that they become cut off from them. This is because you have not nullified your deeds by making this world the goal of your affair. Therefore, it is not permissible for the imam (leader) of the Muslims to agree to a truce with the disbelievers while he has the strength to repel them, and it is not lawful for him to abandon jihad except for a reason in which consideration for the Muslims is evident. If he does not wage jihad in the way of God, his might will turn against the Muslims.

[p. 263]

When he had completed the first reason, he turned to the second: that which turns people away from obedience, leads to disobedience, suits desire, nullifies deeds, and brings about negligence, which in turn leads to the absence of forgiveness. So he said, encouraging obedience to Him, which brings lasting success, by showing how short the days of trial are and how bitter the hardships of toil are: ﴿Indeed, the life of this world﴾. He pointed to its lowliness, to make people averse to it, by saying: ﴿the world﴾. Since absolute elevation (al-'uluw) necessarily brings the greatest pleasure, how much more so when its source is the religion that guarantees the lasting of pleasure, with its worldly and otherworldly aspects joined together [mawsulan]. Play (la'ib) is what arises from an increase of expansiveness (al-bast) and ends quickly, and it also indicates lightness, as in dancing. He placed it first, to indicate that the intelligent person is one who strives for an increase of expansiveness that induces gravity and endures. He followed it with amusement (lahw), which is what joy is sought through, such as singing. This indicates that if what is meant by "the world" is the increase of its expansiveness, then it ends quickly, along with the frivolity it contains. If what is meant is the very essence of expansiveness and joy, then with you is that from elevation, which you attain through jihad, which is at the utmost of greatness, seriousness and permanence. There is no greater foolishness than turning away from it to what, if it gladdens, provokes levity and ends quickly. So He said: ﴿play﴾, that is, lowly, worthless deeds that increase joy, whose dissolution is swift, so they are nullified without fruit. ﴿And amusement﴾, that is, a distraction by which the excitement of pleasure is sought, such as singing, and bewilderment and heedlessness. If you (p. 264) follow them, you will disbelieve, become insolent, and become audacious towards God. [And if you disbelieve in Him and are audacious towards Him,] your rewards will be nullified, so you will have neither reward nor wealth, because He nullifies your deeds and your wealth, by making them become forms without meanings.

When He, glorified be He, depicted the world in the most pleasing of its forms to the ignorant and the most bitter of its forms to the intelligent, and its essence is that it is an increase of joy for one who is joyful and a means of attraction for one who is distressed, yet it is swift to pass away, unlike the fruit of unity upon the religion, which is the joy of elevation through Islam, which endures forever, it becomes known that the implied meaning, based on what follows the description of the world, is: the Hereafter is seriousness, action and presence. So if you turn to it, you will believe and be God-fearing, and the world, in its lowliness, should not deceive you away from attaining the Hereafter through the greater and lesser jihad, despite its nobility and the nobility of the Hereafter. [He said, building upon what the context guided to in its estimation]: ﴿And if you believe and fear God﴾, that is, you are wary, so you place between yourselves and His wrath, glorified be He, a shield against fighting His enemies, enduring the scorching blaze of wars, the heat of enjoining good and forbidding evil, and spending wealth in that cause. Then you will be earnest, leaving the amusement and play that lead to disbelief. ﴿He will give you﴾, that is, God, for whose sake you did that, in the Hereafter, ﴿your rewards﴾, that is, (p. 265) the reward of all your deeds, because they are built upon a foundation. Also, because He is self-sufficient, whom nothing diminishes except giving. The verse is of al-ihtibak (a rhetorical device of mutual omission): the mention of the worldly life, amusement and play first indicates the Hereafter and seriousness, which are omitted second; and the mention of faith and piety second indicates the omission of their opposites, disbelief and audacity, first. Its secret is that depicting a matter through the condition of a child or a fool is more forceful in deterring from it for those of lofty aspirations. And the mention of the reward that is bestowed upon fear, which is the act of the resolute, is more helpful in leaving it.

Since the thing played with, the object of amusement, asks the player who is distracted for his wealth and is not satisfied when asked, and so becomes a cause of the loss of his deeds and wealth, He made clear that the One who is worshipped is different in both respects: He gives and does not take anything for Himself; His taking is only by commanding some of you to show kindness to others. So the Exalted said: ﴿And He will not ask of you﴾, that is, God, in this world, ﴿your wealth﴾, that is, for Himself, nor all of it. This implies that if they do not fear God in the manner mentioned, He will set over them one who takes their wealth, in a way that brings out their grudges. Ibn Burjan said: "Whenever they are asked for their wealth, they become stingy. If they are compelled to do so, they are filled with rancor and hatred, and the ruler gets no sincere counsel from them, nor do they get it from the ruler, nor do they get it from one another; and there is discord, and in that is (p. 266) the destruction." This is a warning from Him, glorified be He, of what will happen afterwards, and He never warns of something without it coming to pass by God's will.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 37:

Since man, by reason of the deficiency with which he has been created, may squander all of his wealth in play and amusement through gambling and the like, and that does not restrain him; rather, it only increases his eagerness, in hope that he will win, yet if he were asked for all of his wealth for obedience (to God), he would be stingy. The Exalted said, mentioning this to them, as an admonition about it and an allusion to His forbearance toward them and His love for them, giving the reason for what precedes it: ﴿If He should ask it of you﴾, i.e., all the wealth. Since wealth is sometimes applied to its greater part, He confirmed the meaning by His saying: ﴿and press you﴾, i.e., He would insist in asking you and push the matter to its utmost limit until He would exhaust it, thereby burdening you, ﴿and you would be stingy﴾, so you would not give anything. ﴿And He would bring out﴾, i.e., God, or the verbal noun understood from "you would be stingy" by that asking, ﴿your malice﴾, i.e., your inclination away from it, until the final outcome of that becomes enmity and rancor. The attribution of the malice to their inner selves indicates that every human being, with the deficiency that is his, harbors what he has been created with of malice, except whom the Merciful, the Most Compassionate, protects. Al-Razi said: This is evidence that the servant, if he is withheld in the seasons of good works other than zakat, does not escape from stinginess. Thus, the definition of stinginess is withholding what the Sharia and manly honor approve of, so it is necessary to observe manly honor and to remove the ugliness of ill repute, and this differs according to differences among individuals. He (al-Razi) put forward the matter that whenever it becomes apparent to him that the benefit of giving is greater than the benefit of withholding, and then giving becomes difficult for him, he is a miser who loves wealth; wealth should not be loved for its own sake but for its benefit. Preserving manly honor is greater, better and stronger than indulging in eating a great deal, for example.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 47, verse 38:

When He informed them of their stinginess should they be asked for all or most of their wealth, He pointed to it by [mentioning] those among them who are stingy regarding what He asked of them, which is a very small portion of their wealth. He said, alerting them to the excellence of His management for them and His pardon of them, according to those who make "ها" (ha) a particle of alerting (tanbih), and according to those who make the hamza of interrogation into "ha," making it for rebuke and reproach, because it is the right of one whom his Master calls to hasten to respond joyfully, let alone to be stingy. In the particle of alerting, especially according to those who see it as repeated, there is emphasis to show how unlikely they are, that anyone would be stingy with what Allah, glorified is He, commands: ﴿Behold, you are those who are called﴾. He belittled their matter, or brought it to mind and depicted it with His words: ﴿you are those who are called﴾, meaning: to your Lord, who does not desire by calling you anything but your benefit, while He Himself is neither reached by benefit nor harm. ﴿to spend﴾ a small portion of the zakat, which is a quarter of a tenth and the like, and of the expenditure for the raid, from which often more than its multiple is obtained from the spoils, and often more than it or [its equal] is obtained from trade. This, and other things, is generalized by His saying ﴿in the way of Allah﴾, meaning: the Greatest King, whose good is hoped for and whose harm is feared, unlike one who is for play and amusement.

When He informed of their being called, He divided them, saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among you﴾, meaning: you who are called, ﴿is one who is stingy﴾, and he is undoubtedly of you. He omitted the other division, which is "and among you is one who is generous," because the purpose is to infer from it what preceded regarding stinginess. Since his stinginess toward the One who gave him wealth, with a small part of it, is only sought so that what is sought from him occurs, the wonder increased with His saying: ﴿And whoever﴾, meaning: while the case is that whoever ﴿is stingy﴾ with that, ﴿then he is only stingy﴾, meaning: with his wealth, stinginess issuing ﴿from himself﴾, which is the source of baseness, so there is no grasping or competing except for a base thing; for the benefit of that which was asked of him and he withheld is only for himself. He emphasized it because hardly anyone believes that a sensible person would sacrifice his wealth at the expense of his own benefit. For this reason He omitted: "And whoever is generous, is only generous toward himself," because it is understood from the context, and the evidence makes it unnecessary. This being said, the better view is that ﴿yabkhal﴾ (is stingy) implies ﴿yumsik﴾ (withholds), then ﴿yumsik﴾ was omitted and indicated by an omitted state, indicated by the transitivity with ʿan.

Since asking for wealth may give rise to some misunderstanding, He said, removing it, establishing that the stinginess of a person is only toward himself, conjoining it to what is implied: because the harm of his stinginess returns only to him, and He, glorified is He, did not ask you for that out of need for it, nor for anything from you, but for your need of reward. He, glorified is He, has built the affairs of this abode upon causes as wisdom requires: ﴿And Allah﴾, meaning: the Greatest King, to whom belongs encompassing all attributes of perfection, ﴿is the Self-Sufficient﴾, meaning: alone, ﴿while you﴾, O you who are charged specifically, ﴿are the poor﴾, because giving benefits you and withholding harms you. So whoever of you becomes needy toward one like himself falls into humiliation and degradation. Your custom has been that joy enters you, which you do not find, when one of you asks anything from one of the generous rich, hoping for his reward. So be like that and greater, when you are asked for absolute richness.

Since the sense was: "If you accept [this] with your gift, you will prosper," He conjoined to it His saying, instilling dread, because dread is more restraining: ﴿And if you turn away﴾, meaning: if you anticipate turning away from it, you will burden yourselves against what the first nature calls to, namely allowing that very small reward which entails great reward and everlasting success, and from jihad in His way and standing in His obedience, because He is the Benefactor, and there is no real benefactor other than Him. ﴿He will substitute﴾, meaning: He will bring into being ﴿a people﴾ among whom there is strength and sufficiency for what is asked of them to attempt.

Since that implies that they are other than them, yet this does not prevent that they might be, while being other than their persons, from their own people, or that He might make them superior to them in attributes even if they are not of their people, He pointed out that they would be not of their people and not of their attributes, rather they would be higher than them in rank, more noble in disposition, and better in deed. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿other than you﴾, meaning: in place of you, and this is not in the attribute of turning away.

Since people are close in natural dispositions, and wealth is beloved, it was very unlikely that this giving would be other than what they are upon. Exalted is He said, indicating that with the particle of delay as emphasis for what the saying "other than" conveyed, and as confirmation of it: ﴿then﴾, meaning: after the remoteness of what is deemed remote and the elevation of resolve in passing over all the obstacles of the self and Satan: ﴿they will not be like you﴾ in turning away from Him by leaving something of what He commanded or doing something of what He forbade. Whoever is able to bring into being is able to annihilate.

Indeed, it is easier in the courses of customary affairs. It is established that, were He to will, He, glorified is He, would have taken revenge upon the disbelievers, either by destroying them or by others besides you striking their necks, taking them captive, and other such matters. And it is established by the continuous censure of the disbelievers, despite His power over them, that He nullified their deeds. Thus the beginning of the surah returns to its end, and its conclusion embraces what you see of its detail. It is known that the meaning of this last and that first is: He, glorified is He, must humiliate the disbelievers and exalt the believers, for if they turn toward what pleases Him and strive, He will grant them a mighty victory, by what His saying, exalted is He, guarantees: ﴿If you help Allah, He will help you and make your feet firm﴾ [Muhammad: 7]. And if you turn away, He will bring a people other than you who turn toward Him, and He will fulfill His promise to them, so their abandonment becomes an inevitable matter, and this is the meaning of the beginning of Surah Muhammad. And Allah is the Granter of success for what He wills of what is right.
